content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Secure Data Sharing
Secure Data Sharing with Snowflake
Share live, governed data without ETL, keeping control where the data lives.
Orientation

Snowflake shares provide read-only, live access to provider data. Providers define a share object that lists databases, schemas, and tables. Consumers create a database from that share and query it like a local read-only database.

In this lesson: create a share, grant USAGE and SELECT, add accounts, then create a database from the share.
Explore Key Topics
Share Object
Defines which databases, schemas, tables, and consumer accounts can access provider data.
Consumer DB
Created with CREATE DATABASE ... FROM SHARE. Read-only, live view into provider data.
Security
Grant USAGE and SELECT only. Audit shares regularly and apply least privilege.
Provider
Owns data
Creates share, grants USAGE and SELECT, adds consumer accounts.
Account: ORGABC.ACCOUNT67890
No data movement — live references only
Consumer
Reads shared data
Creates database from share, queries live, read-only data.
Account: ORG1.ACCOUNTXYZ
Coming up
A hands-on example will build a sample PRODUCT_CATALOG table, create a share, grant the right privileges, add a consumer account, and then show the consumer creating a database from that share to query live rows.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the fundamental concept of Snowflake data sharing and why providers can share live data without copying it. Second, you will identify the two core roles in sharing — the provider who owns the data and the consumer who receives read-only access — and learn the responsibilities of each role. Third, you will create and manage secure shares: you’ll use CREATE SHARE, grant USAGE on database and schema, and grant SELECT on tables or views. Fourth, you will consume shared data by creating a database from a share and querying it. Each objective ties to commands and a hands-on example so you can practice. Throughout we emphasize security: apply least privilege and audit shares regularly. By the end you should be able to set up a simple share, troubleshoot a common USAGE grant mistake, and consume shared data while preserving provider control.

screens.title: What is Secure Data Sharing?
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake's secure data sharing lets a provider account expose selected databases, schemas, tables, or views to consumer accounts without copying data. That means the provider keeps control of physical data while consumers get a live, read-only view. The main benefits are reduced ETL, no file movement, and always-current information. For example, a sales team can expose the SALES_ORDERS table to marketing; marketing creates a database from the share and runs queries against current orders without the provider exporting files. A common misconception is that sharing moves or duplicates data — it does not. Another pitfall is assuming consumers can write to shared tables; shared databases are read-only from the consumer side. A practical takeaway is to model shares like access windows: define exactly what should be visible and test the consumer experience so they can query expected rows. As a quick check, remember that consumers will always see provider updates immediately, so coordinate any schema changes and communicate versioning to consumers to avoid breaking queries. What is Secure Data Sharing? means secure data sharing exposes live, read-only views of provider data to consumers, eliminating copying while keeping provider control.. In practical terms, definition, benefits, and a practical example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is Secure Data Sharing?
Definition
A provider grants read-only, live access to specific objects by creating a share; consumers create a database from that share to query current data.
Why it matters
  • Eliminates ETL and file transfers between accounts.
  • Consumers always query up-to-date rows; no stale copies.
  • Providers maintain data governance and control.
Key Takeaway

Model shares as windows into provider data. Share intentionally and test consumer queries to confirm results and access behavior.

Concrete example
A sales account exposes the SALES_ORDERS table to a marketing account. Marketing runs analytics immediately without any copy. Provider still controls who sees which columns and can revoke access any time.
Misconception
Sharing is not data movement. Consumers do not own or store the shared rows; they only gain read-only visibility to live provider data.

screens.title: Provider vs Consumer
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding roles is foundational. The data provider is the Snowflake account that owns the source data and creates the share object. The provider chooses which databases, schemas, tables, or views to include and which consumer accounts may access the share. Providers must grant USAGE on the database and schema and SELECT on the objects to the share. They retain full control over lifecycle and can revoke access. The data consumer is the account that receives authorization. A consumer creates a database from a share and queries it as a read-only database. Consumers cannot perform INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE on shared objects — a common source of confusion. A concrete example: ORGABC. ACCOUNT67890 shares SALES_ANALYTICS. PUBLIC. SALES_ORDERS; ORG1. ACCOUNTXYZ creates sales_data_from_provider and runs analytics. Misconception to avoid: consumers cannot change provider data. Takeaway: design shares so providers expose only what consumers need and document the intended consumer workflows. Provider vs Consumer means provider owns and controls data and privileges; consumer gets read-only, live access and cannot modify shared objects.. In practical terms, roles, privileges, and limitations contrasted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Provider vs Consumer
Provider (owner)
  • Creates the share object with CREATE SHARE.
  • Grants USAGE on database/schema and SELECT on tables/views to the share.
  • Adds consumer accounts with ALTER SHARE ... ADD ACCOUNTS.
  • Retains control and can revoke access any time.
Example account id: ORGABC.ACCOUNT67890
Consumer (reader)
  • Creates a database from the share with CREATE DATABASE ... FROM SHARE.
  • Queries shared tables as read-only objects.
  • Sees live, current data; provider updates are immediately visible.
  • Cannot perform DML operations on shared objects.
Example account id: ORG1.ACCOUNTXYZ
Common mistake
Assuming consumers can modify shared data. Shared databases are read-only for consumers; any data changes must happen in the provider account.

screens.title: Provider: Create a Share
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a share is a small set of clear steps with important order. First, create the share object with CREATE SHARE and give it a meaningful name. Second, grant USAGE on the database that contains the objects you plan to share. Third, grant USAGE on the schema inside that database so the consumer can navigate to objects. Fourth, grant SELECT on the specific tables or views to the share. These SELECT privileges are the only object privileges you grant to allow reading. Finally, add the consumer account identifier to the share with ALTER SHARE... ADD ACCOUNTS. A frequent mistake is granting SELECT but forgetting the USAGE grants on the parent database and schema; without those, consumers cannot reach the table even though SELECT exists. Example commands follow the same pattern used in practice. Always verify with SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE and DESCRIBE SHARE to confirm the expected objects and accounts are listed before announcing access to consumers. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Create a Share
Step-by-step
  1. Create the share object with CREATE SHARE.
  2. Grant USAGE on the database to the share.
  3. Grant USAGE on the schema to the share.
  4. Grant SELECT on the specific tables or views to the share.
  5. Add consumer accounts to the share with ALTER SHARE ... ADD ACCOUNTS.
Common mistake
Granting SELECT without USAGE on the database/schema prevents consumers from navigating to the objects.
Example SQL
-- As ACCOUNTADMIN or role with CREATE SHARE
CREATE SHARE my_sales_share;

-- Grants to the share
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE SALES_DB TO SHARE my_sales_share;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA SALES_DB.PUBLIC_SCHEMA TO SHARE my_sales_share;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE SALES_DB.PUBLIC_SCHEMA.SALES_ORDERS TO SHARE my_sales_share;

-- Add the consumer account
ALTER SHARE my_sales_share ADD ACCOUNTS = 'ORG1.ACCOUNTXYZ';
Tip: run SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE my_sales_share to verify.

screens.title: Granting Privileges — details and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Privilege granting is the core of secure sharing. The provider must grant USAGE on the database and the schema to the share; these container grants let the consumer find the objects. Then grant SELECT on each table or view you want to expose. Only SELECT is appropriate for tables and views in a share because consumers must not modify provider data. A common error is granting ALL PRIVILEGES or other broad rights; doing so can expose more than intended and violate least-privilege principles. Another trap is forgetting to grant schema-level USAGE when you have already granted database-level USAGE. When in doubt, audit with SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE and DESCRIBE SHARE. If a consumer reports they cannot see a table, check for missing USAGE on both database and schema before changing object privileges. Document exactly which objects are shared and consider secure views or masking for sensitive columns. These practices keep sharing safe and predictable. Granting Privileges — details and pitfalls means grant usage on database and schema, then select on objects. avoid all privileges; follow least privilege.. In practical terms, usage on containers and select on objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Granting Privileges
What to grant
  • USAGE on the provider database to the share.
  • USAGE on the provider schema to the share.
  • SELECT on each table or view to the share.
Pitfall
Granting ALL PRIVILEGES or other elevated rights can unintentionally expose data. Stick to USAGE and SELECT.
Verify and audit
After granting, run SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE my_share and DESCRIBE SHARE my_share to confirm which objects and accounts are associated with the share. If a consumer cannot access a table, first confirm USAGE exists on both the database and schema.
Key Takeaway

Privilege grants must complete a path from database → schema → object for consumers to navigate and query shared data.

screens.title: Adding Consumer Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: After defining a share and granting object privileges, you must add consumer accounts so those accounts can create a database from the share. The provider runs ALTER SHARE my_share ADD ACCOUNTS = 'ACCOUNT_IDENTIFIER'. The account identifier is a Snowflake account name like ORG1. ACCOUNTXYZ. Always confirm you have the exact identifier from the consumer; a typo prevents access and can be hard to diagnose. Once added, the consumer will see the share and can create a database from it. A validation checklist helps: confirm the share lists the account via DESCRIBE SHARE, confirm USAGE and SELECT grants were applied, and ask the consumer to try CREATE DATABASE FROM SHARE. If the consumer cannot create the database, confirm the account was added correctly and that the consumer user has CREATE DATABASE permission in their own account. Clear communication between provider and consumer about identifiers and roles saves time and reduces errors. Adding Consumer Accounts means add consumer accounts precisely with alter share ... add accounts and verify with describe share; confirm consumer can run create database from share.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Add Consumer Accounts
Command example
-- Add a consumer account to the share
ALTER SHARE partner_product_share ADD ACCOUNTS = 'YOUR_PARTNER_ACCOUNT_IDENTIFIER';

-- Verify the share
DESCRIBE SHARE partner_product_share;
SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE partner_product_share;
Tip: request the exact account identifier string from the consumer to avoid typos.
Validation checklist
  • DESCRIBE SHARE shows the consumer account listed.
  • SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE lists the database, schema, and object grants.
  • Consumer can run CREATE DATABASE FROM SHARE and query objects.
Common issue
Consumer gets an error creating the database: often the provider failed to add the exact account identifier or the consumer lacks CREATE DATABASE privileges internally.

screens.title: Consumer: Create Database from Share
screens.narratorSegment: On the consumer side, once the provider has added your account, you create a shared database with CREATE DATABASE... FROM SHARE using the provider’s account identifier and the share name. This creates a read-only database in your account that references the provider’s objects. After creation, you can run standard SELECT queries against shared tables just like local objects; remember these queries hit live provider data. A concrete example: CREATE DATABASE sales_data_from_provider FROM SHARE ORG1. ACCOUNT12345. my_sales_share. Then run SELECT * FROM sales_data_from_provider. PUBLIC_SCHEMA. SALES_ORDERS to see rows. A common misconception is that the data will perform the same as local tables; performance depends on provider-side settings and compute usage patterns. Also confirm the consumer role has CREATE DATABASE privileges locally before attempting to create the shared database. Finally, treat the shared database as read-only and coordinate schema changes with the provider to avoid breaking consumer queries. screens.title: Live Data and Read-Only Semantics
screens.narratorSegment: When Snowflake shares data, 'live' means consumers query the provider’s current state — no intermediate snapshots are created by the sharing mechanism itself. This has operational implications. For providers, any updates, deletes, or schema changes are immediately visible to consumers. That requires coordination: announce schema changes and use versioning or views where appropriate to avoid breaking consumer queries. For consumers, remember you cannot change shared objects; you must request changes from the provider or build local copies if modification is needed. A common misunderstanding is to treat shared data like a static copy; instead, treat it like a live feed. If your workload requires isolated, writeable copies, use standard data ingestion to create local tables. Otherwise, using shared live data reduces duplication and keeps everyone aligned to a single source of truth. A final tip: use secure views or masking to hide or transform sensitive columns while still allowing useful access. screens.title: Security Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security should guide every sharing decision. The principle of least privilege asks you to grant only what consumers need: USAGE on database and schema, and SELECT on specific tables or views. Avoid granting broad rights like ALL PRIVILEGES. For sensitive data, consider creating secure views that expose only required columns or using dynamic data masking to hide or obfuscate sensitive values; the chapter notes that masking is covered later, but planning for it now helps. Regularly audit shares with SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE and DESCRIBE SHARE to confirm which objects and accounts are listed and to detect unintended grants. Maintain an approval workflow for creating shares, and log communications about who requested access and why. A common operational error is accidental exposure due to overbroad grants — preventing this requires clear policies, peer review of share configurations, and periodic reviews. Security Best Practices means grant minimal privileges, protect sensitive columns with views or masking, and audit shares regularly to maintain secure sharing posture.. screens.title: Data Exchanges and Marketplace
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond direct sharing between accounts, Snowflake supports data exchanges and a Marketplace. A data exchange is a private environment where a group of accounts can share datasets within an agreed ecosystem; it simplifies sharing among many related accounts without adding each account individually to a share. The Marketplace enables providers to list datasets publicly or privately for discovery and consumption by a broader audience. For certification-level tasks we focus on direct shares, but understanding exchanges and the Marketplace helps design larger ecosystems. A typical use case for exchanges is when a consortium of partners needs shared access to common reference sets; for Marketplace listings, a provider wants discoverability and possibly monetization. Key governance differences include discovery, onboarding flows, and potential commercial agreements. Always assess whether direct sharing, an exchange, or a Marketplace listing best fits privacy, control, and discoverability needs. screens.title: Hands-on: Share a PRODUCT_CATALOG
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the hands-on scenario end-to-end. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hands-on: PRODUCT_CATALOG
Provider steps (example)
CREATE DATABASE SALES_ANALYTICS;
CREATE SCHEMA SALES_ANALYTICS.PUBLIC;

USE DATABASE SALES_ANALYTICS;
USE SCHEMA PUBLIC;
CREATE TABLE PRODUCT_CATALOG (
  PRODUCT_ID INT,
  PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR(255),
  CATEGORY VARCHAR(100),
  PRICE DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
INSERT INTO PRODUCT_CATALOG VALUES
(1, 'Laptop Pro', 'Electronics', 1200.00),
(2, 'Wireless Mouse', 'Accessories', 25.00),
(3, 'Mechanical Keyboard', 'Accessories', 90.00);

CREATE SHARE partner_product_share;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE SALES_ANALYTICS TO SHARE partner_product_share;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA SALES_ANALYTICS.PUBLIC TO SHARE partner_product_share;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE SALES_ANALYTICS.PUBLIC.PRODUCT_CATALOG TO SHARE partner_product_share;
ALTER SHARE partner_product_share ADD ACCOUNTS = 'YOUR_PARTNER_ACCOUNT_IDENTIFIER';
Run these as a role with CREATE SHARE privilege.
Consumer steps (example)
-- As consumer with CREATE DATABASE privilege
CREATE DATABASE shared_products FROM SHARE YOUR_PROVIDER_ACCOUNT_IDENTIFIER.partner_product_share;
USE DATABASE shared_products;
SELECT * FROM PUBLIC.PRODUCT_CATALOG;
Expected output: three product rows returned from the provider's table, reflecting live data.
Lab check
If the consumer sees no rows, confirm the provider granted USAGE on both database and schema and added the correct account identifier to the share.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Snowflake lets one account share live data with another without copying or moving files. I’ll explain the provider and consumer roles, the share object that defines which databases, schemas, and tables are exposed, and the basic sequence of commands a provider and consumer use to enable sharing. You will see why this approach removes ETL overhead, reduces stale copies, and keeps control in the provider account. I’ll also point out common mistakes, like forgetting to grant USAGE on the database or schema, and why the principle of least privilege matters. By the end, you’ll understand the workflow from creating a share to querying a shared database, and you’ll be prepared to follow the hands-on example later that walks through creating a sample table, granting SELECT to a share, adding a consumer account, and creating a database from that share. Consider how live, read-only access changes the way teams collaborate and how auditing and secure views help keep sensitive columns protected.

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the fundamental concept of Snowflake data sharing and why providers can share live data without copying it. Second, you will identify the two core roles in sharing — the provider who owns the data and the consumer who receives read-only access — and learn the responsibilities of each role. Third, you will create and manage secure shares: you’ll use CREATE SHARE, grant USAGE on database and schema, and grant SELECT on tables or views. Fourth, you will consume shared data by creating a database from a share and querying it. Each objective ties to commands and a hands-on example so you can practice. Throughout we emphasize security: apply least privilege and audit shares regularly. By the end you should be able to set up a simple share, troubleshoot a common USAGE grant mistake, and consume shared data while preserving provider control.

These additional objectives focus on secure operations and troubleshooting. Objective five is to troubleshoot common sharing issues, such as missing USAGE on a database or schema that prevents consumers from navigating to shared tables even when SELECT exists. Objective six is to apply the principle of least privilege when granting access, avoiding ALL PRIVILEGES and granting only USAGE and SELECT as required. Objective seven introduces broader sharing mechanisms: understand the difference between direct account-to-account shares, data exchanges, and the Marketplace listing model. Objective eight is to audit shares and use SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE and DESCRIBE SHARE to verify configurations. Together these skills ensure you can share useful data without exposing more than intended and maintain compliance through regular review. Learning Objectives — continued means troubleshooting, least-privilege granting, exchanges vs direct shares, and auditing are essential for secure, compliant data sharing.. In practical terms, security, troubleshooting, and governance goals. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Snowflake's secure data sharing lets a provider account expose selected databases, schemas, tables, or views to consumer accounts without copying data. That means the provider keeps control of physical data while consumers get a live, read-only view. The main benefits are reduced ETL, no file movement, and always-current information. For example, a sales team can expose the SALES_ORDERS table to marketing; marketing creates a database from the share and runs queries against current orders without the provider exporting files. A common misconception is that sharing moves or duplicates data — it does not. Another pitfall is assuming consumers can write to shared tables; shared databases are read-only from the consumer side. A practical takeaway is to model shares like access windows: define exactly what should be visible and test the consumer experience so they can query expected rows. As a quick check, remember that consumers will always see provider updates immediately, so coordinate any schema changes and communicate versioning to consumers to avoid breaking queries. What is Secure Data Sharing? means secure data sharing exposes live, read-only views of provider data to consumers, eliminating copying while keeping provider control.. In practical terms, definition, benefits, and a practical example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding roles is foundational. The data provider is the Snowflake account that owns the source data and creates the share object. The provider chooses which databases, schemas, tables, or views to include and which consumer accounts may access the share. Providers must grant USAGE on the database and schema and SELECT on the objects to the share. They retain full control over lifecycle and can revoke access. The data consumer is the account that receives authorization. A consumer creates a database from a share and queries it as a read-only database. Consumers cannot perform INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE on shared objects — a common source of confusion. A concrete example: ORGABC. ACCOUNT67890 shares SALES_ANALYTICS. PUBLIC. SALES_ORDERS; ORG1. ACCOUNTXYZ creates sales_data_from_provider and runs analytics. Misconception to avoid: consumers cannot change provider data. Takeaway: design shares so providers expose only what consumers need and document the intended consumer workflows. Provider vs Consumer means provider owns and controls data and privileges; consumer gets read-only, live access and cannot modify shared objects.. In practical terms, roles, privileges, and limitations contrasted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating a share is a small set of clear steps with important order. First, create the share object with CREATE SHARE and give it a meaningful name. Second, grant USAGE on the database that contains the objects you plan to share. Third, grant USAGE on the schema inside that database so the consumer can navigate to objects. Fourth, grant SELECT on the specific tables or views to the share. These SELECT privileges are the only object privileges you grant to allow reading. Finally, add the consumer account identifier to the share with ALTER SHARE... ADD ACCOUNTS. A frequent mistake is granting SELECT but forgetting the USAGE grants on the parent database and schema; without those, consumers cannot reach the table even though SELECT exists. Example commands follow the same pattern used in practice. Always verify with SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE and DESCRIBE SHARE to confirm the expected objects and accounts are listed before announcing access to consumers. Provider: Create a Share means order matters: create share → grant usage on database → grant usage on schema → grant select on objects → alter share add accounts.. In practical terms, commands to define a share and grant privileges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Privilege granting is the core of secure sharing. The provider must grant USAGE on the database and the schema to the share; these container grants let the consumer find the objects. Then grant SELECT on each table or view you want to expose. Only SELECT is appropriate for tables and views in a share because consumers must not modify provider data. A common error is granting ALL PRIVILEGES or other broad rights; doing so can expose more than intended and violate least-privilege principles. Another trap is forgetting to grant schema-level USAGE when you have already granted database-level USAGE. When in doubt, audit with SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE and DESCRIBE SHARE. If a consumer reports they cannot see a table, check for missing USAGE on both database and schema before changing object privileges. Document exactly which objects are shared and consider secure views or masking for sensitive columns. These practices keep sharing safe and predictable. Granting Privileges — details and pitfalls means grant usage on database and schema, then select on objects. avoid all privileges; follow least privilege.. In practical terms, usage on containers and select on objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After defining a share and granting object privileges, you must add consumer accounts so those accounts can create a database from the share. The provider runs ALTER SHARE my_share ADD ACCOUNTS = 'ACCOUNT_IDENTIFIER'. The account identifier is a Snowflake account name like ORG1. ACCOUNTXYZ. Always confirm you have the exact identifier from the consumer; a typo prevents access and can be hard to diagnose. Once added, the consumer will see the share and can create a database from it. A validation checklist helps: confirm the share lists the account via DESCRIBE SHARE, confirm USAGE and SELECT grants were applied, and ask the consumer to try CREATE DATABASE FROM SHARE. If the consumer cannot create the database, confirm the account was added correctly and that the consumer user has CREATE DATABASE permission in their own account. Clear communication between provider and consumer about identifiers and roles saves time and reduces errors. Adding Consumer Accounts means add consumer accounts precisely with alter share ... add accounts and verify with describe share; confirm consumer can run create database from share.. In practical terms, how to add the correct account identifier and common validation steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

On the consumer side, once the provider has added your account, you create a shared database with CREATE DATABASE... FROM SHARE using the provider’s account identifier and the share name. When Snowflake shares data, 'live' means consumers query the provider’s current state — no intermediate snapshots are created by the sharing mechanism itself. This has operational implications. For providers, any updates, deletes, or schema changes are immediately visible to consumers. That requires coordination: announce schema changes and use versioning or views where appropriate to avoid breaking consumer queries. For consumers, remember you cannot change shared objects; you must request changes from the provider or build local copies if modification is needed. A common misunderstanding is to treat shared data like a static copy; instead, treat it like a live feed. If your workload requires isolated, writeable copies, use standard data ingestion to create local tables. Otherwise, using shared live data reduces duplication and keeps everyone aligned to a single source of truth. A final tip: use secure views or masking to hide or transform sensitive columns while still allowing useful access. Security should guide every sharing decision. The principle of least privilege asks you to grant only what consumers need: USAGE on database and schema, and SELECT on specific tables or views. Avoid granting broad rights like ALL PRIVILEGES. For sensitive data, consider creating secure views that expose only required columns or using dynamic data masking to hide or obfuscate sensitive values; the chapter notes that masking is covered later, but planning for it now helps. Regularly audit shares with SHOW GRANTS OF SHARE and DESCRIBE SHARE to confirm which objects and accounts are listed and to detect unintended grants. Maintain an approval workflow for creating shares, and log communications about who requested access and why. A common operational error is accidental exposure due to overbroad grants — preventing this requires clear policies, peer review of share configurations, and periodic reviews. Beyond direct sharing between accounts, Snowflake supports data exchanges and a Marketplace. A data exchange is a private environment where a group of accounts can share datasets within an agreed ecosystem; it simplifies sharing among many related accounts without adding each account individually to a share. The Marketplace enables providers to list datasets publicly or privately for discovery and consumption by a broader audience. For certification-level tasks we focus on direct shares, but understanding exchanges and the Marketplace helps design larger ecosystems. A typical use case for exchanges is when a consortium of partners needs shared access to common reference sets; for Marketplace listings, a provider wants discoverability and possibly monetization. Key governance differences include discovery, onboarding flows, and potential commercial agreements. Always assess whether direct sharing, an exchange, or a Marketplace listing best fits privacy, control, and discoverability needs. Let's summarize the key concepts you should retain. First, a share object is the provider-created definition of which databases, schemas, tables, and views are available to consumer accounts; data does not move. Second, the shared database that the consumer creates is read-only and reflects live provider data — consumers cannot modify shared objects. Third, privilege granting is hierarchical: you must grant USAGE on the database and schema and SELECT on objects for consumers to navigate and query the data. Keep these three points in mind as you design shares and govern access. Also remember to follow least-privilege principles, audit shares regularly, and coordinate schema changes between providers and consumers to avoid breaking queries.
